Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: For a man-made disaster trauma in a 58-year-old forensic analyst, this item is only coherent if there was a significant physical injury. The rest of the selected profile does not support an injury-based presentation: the threat items emphasize environmental danger and vigilance (limited safe places, loud sounds, unfamiliar places), while the other appraisals are about coping failure and loss of capability rather than concrete bodily injury. With no memory or strategy items to anchor a physical-injury narrative, this appraisal stands out as clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with the supplied cognitive formulation because all cross-node edges are inactive, which implies these components should not appear as tightly linked aspects of one maintaining pattern. However, the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items are strongly conceptually connected: perceiving the world as dangerous maps directly onto restricted safety zones and avoidance of unfamiliar places, creating an active Threat–Negative Appraisal linkage that contradicts the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within the selected nodes, the content clusters into a classic mutually reinforcing danger/coping pattern rather than isolated components. 'World is a dangerous place' coheres directly with hypervigilance to sounds and avoidance of unfamiliar places, while 'Bad Coper' and 'No longer capable' reflect generalized post-trauma self-evaluation likely tied to the same threat response. With no active edges anywhere in the formulation, this degree of integration is inconsistent.

issues.item: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: The formulation specifies no active edges, so the selected nodes should function as relatively isolated components rather than implying a tight linked syndrome. Here the Threat items and Negative Appraisal items form a classic connected PTSD pattern: danger-focused hypervigilance/startle and avoidance are closely mirrored by broad beliefs that the world is dangerous and that the self is incapable. This actively implies strong Threat↔Negative Appraisal linkage, which contradicts the fully disconnected formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Within Threat, the items are coherent with each other, and within Negative Appraisals the items are also coherent. The problem is cross-node/formulation consistency: the profile presents mutually reinforcing danger sensitivity and negative self/world beliefs despite all edges being inactive.

vignette:
Rodrigo Mendes is a 58-year-old forensic analyst of Colombian descent who has spent the better part of three decades studying the aftermath of violence with a professional detachment he once considered one of his defining strengths. He is married, the father of two adult children, and until approximately fourteen months ago, he was the kind of man who walked into a crime scene the way other people walk into a familiar room - purposeful, composed, certain of what he would find and how he would respond to it. That certainty ended on the afternoon a gas main explosion tore through a municipal building two blocks from the county forensics lab where he works, a disaster that killed eleven people and left Rodrigo standing in the street amid collapsing facades, screaming sirens, and the particular quality of silence that follows a pressure wave - the few seconds when the world seems to have forgotten how to make sound. He had been outside on a routine errand. The force of the blast knocked him from his feet. When he got up, the street he had walked a hundred times looked like something from the case files on his desk, and for a moment he could not locate himself in it at all.

In the weeks that followed, Rodrigo found that his body had not returned with him to the life he had before. He began waking in the early hours with his heart already racing, his muscles braced for impact, as though his nervous system had decided that sleep was a lapse in vigilance he could not afford. At the lab, the sudden bang of a heavy door or the percussive thud of a colleague dropping a binder was enough to send a visible flinch through him - a response he found humiliating in a man whose professional identity had been built on steadiness. He began to feel, at all times, that his body was running a threat calculation he had not authorised, scanning for danger in the fluorescent corridors of a building he had entered without anxiety for twenty-two years.

Outside the lab, the hypervigilance extended further. Rodrigo stopped accepting assignments that required site visits to unfamiliar locations, telling supervisors he preferred to work from recovered materials. In truth, the thought of entering a space he had not already mentally mapped - a building he did not know the exits of, a neighbourhood whose sightlines he could not read - produced a dread so immediate that avoidance felt less like a choice than a necessity. His world contracted. The drive to work, the lab itself, the route home: these were the coordinates of a life that had grown very small.

What troubled Rodrigo as much as the symptoms themselves was what he had come to believe they meant about him. He had spent his career analysing scenes of catastrophe with precision and calm; he had always assumed that if something terrible happened to him personally, he would process it with the same professional efficiency. Instead, he found himself jumpy, avoidant, unable to walk into an unfamiliar parking structure without his chest tightening. He was certain, in a way that resisted argument, that this constituted evidence of a fundamental deficiency - that his reactions since the explosion showed him to be, as he put it in his intake session, "a lousy coper." More painful still was the sense that the competence which had defined him was simply gone. The forensic analyst who could hold a scene of mass death at an interpretable distance no longer existed, and Rodrigo did not know what remained in his place. He had come to believe, quietly and with great conviction, that the world was a more dangerous place than he had previously understood - not in the abstract way a professional understands risk, but in the visceral, bodily way of a man who knows what a pressure wave feels like from the inside.

It was his wife, Claudia, who finally persuaded him to seek help after he declined to attend their grandson's birthday party at an unfamiliar event venue - a refusal that landed between them with the weight of something irreversible. Rodrigo came to his first session hoping, above all, to be told that the man he had been was still recoverable. What he feared most was that the answer was no.
